data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Ownership-based allocation systematically suppresses cross-cutting explanations by denying rival lineages the chance to translate problems into their own vocabularies, thereby preventing the 'reframing' that often reveals a simpler or more unifying structural pattern.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If L_owner's grammar is already a 'universal grammar' that can derive all rival primitives as theorems, then L_rival's translation would add no new information and suppression is indistinguishable from efficiency.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If problems in the run are intrinsically non-cross-cutting (each belongs to one and only one structural family), then L_rival would fail to find a simpler pattern anyway and no suppression occurs.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If L_owner's own search includes an exhaustive meta-step that explicitly tests reframings of p into all known rival grammars, then the ownership barrier is harmless.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"An owning lineage L_owner processes problem p using its own established primitives. Because rival lineage L_rival is structurally barred from attempting p, it never translates p's constraints into L_rival's vocabulary. Translation is the exact step where a cross-cutting explanation would emerge: L_rival would see that p's surface features map to a known structural pattern in L_rival's domain that L_owner lacks. By construction, L_owner's vocabulary will confirm its own primitives are sufficient (or fail), but will never detect that L_rival's grammar subsumes the problem more elegantly. The suppression is thus not a side-effect but a direct causal consequence of partitioning the problem space by provenance.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
